meta.title: Snakes & Ladders
meta.subtitle: Scale from a local Dockerfile to global GKE Autopilot & Cloud Run fleets — master autoscaling, service mesh, supply chain & probes.
meta.author: Google Cloud Architecture

1.title: Local Dockerfile & Port 8080 Prototype
1.quip: "It runs on my laptop with `docker run -p 8080:8080`—zero health probes, `:latest` tags, and big multi-region dreams."
1.tip: Start with minimal distroless base images, stateless 12-factor configuration, explicit CPU/memory requests, and graceful SIGTERM handling.

100.title: Zero-Ops Global GKE & Cloud Run Fleet!
100.quip: "Multi-cluster GKE Gateway, sub-second Cloud Run scale-out, SLSA Level 3 Binary Authorization, and zero pod eviction pages."
100.tip: World-class container platforms combine GKE Autopilot, Cloud Run Services/Jobs, Gateway API traffic management, Workload Identity, and practiced canary rollbacks.

ladders.title: GKE Autopilot Pod-Based Billing & Hardened Nodes
ladders.quip: "Stopped paying for idle node slack and stopped patching worker VMs—you now pay strictly for running Pod vCPU and memory requests!"
ladders.tip: Use GKE Autopilot for fully managed node provisioning, pre-hardened security defaults, and per-Pod resource billing.
ladders.q: How does GKE Autopilot differ from GKE Standard in cluster operations and billing?
opts: Google manages and hardens worker nodes automatically, and you are billed only for the vCPU, memory, and ephemeral storage requested by your running Pods
You must manually SSH into worker nodes every week to upgrade the Linux kernel and kubelet
Autopilot only supports Windows Server 2012 virtual machines without containers
ladders.why: GKE Autopilot eliminates node pool management and bin-packing waste by billing directly for Pod resource requests with enforced security baselines.

ladders.title: GKE Compute Classes & Node Auto-Provisioning
ladders.quip: "GPU inference pods and high-memory jobs automatically provisioned dedicated right-sized node pools and scaled them to zero when finished."
ladders.tip: Use Custom Compute Classes or Node Auto-Provisioning (NAP) to dynamically select optimal machine series (such as C3, N2, or Spot/GPU) based on Pod selectors.
ladders.docLabel: About Custom Compute Classes in GKE
ladders.q: What capability do GKE Custom Compute Classes provide when scheduling diverse workloads?
opts: They force all Pods across the organization to run on a single e2-micro VM
They declaratively define fallback priorities across machine families, Spot VMs, and reservations so GKE provisions the best available compute automatically
They disable the Kubernetes scheduler and assign Pods randomly via DNS
ladders.why: Custom Compute Classes let platform teams define prioritized hardware/Spot fallback chains so GKE automatically provisions optimal nodes as capacity demands shift.

ladders.title: Multidimensional Pod Autoscaling (HPA + VPA)
ladders.quip: "Scaled replicas horizontally on Pub/Sub queue depth while VPA right-sized memory requests automatically!"
ladders.tip: Combine Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (scaling replica count on CPU or custom metrics) with Vertical Pod Autoscaler for memory sizing, or use Multidimensional Pod Autoscaler.
ladders.q: When combining horizontal and vertical scaling on the same Deployment in GKE, how do you prevent HPA and VPA from fighting each other?
opts: Configure HPA and VPA to both scale replica count and CPU limits simultaneously every second
Delete all resource requests from the Pod spec
Use Multidimensional Pod Autoscaler (or scale horizontally on CPU/custom requests while VPA manages memory requests in recommendation/auto mode)
ladders.why: If HPA and VPA both react to the same CPU utilization signal independently, they conflict; separating dimensions (HPA on CPU/custom metrics, VPA on memory) or using Multidimensional Pod Autoscaler coordinates both.

ladders.title: GKE Image Streaming from Artifact Registry
ladders.quip: "A 4 GB ML inference container booted in 3 seconds instead of 90 seconds by streaming layers on demand over the network!"
ladders.tip: Enable Image Streaming on GKE with Artifact Registry in the same region so containers start before downloading the entire image tarball.
ladders.q: How does GKE Image Streaming reduce Pod startup latency for large container images?
opts: It mounts container layers over a virtual filesystem from Artifact Registry and fetches only the blocks actually read during startup while streaming the rest in the background
It deletes all shared libraries larger than 10 MB from the container image
It emails the container image as a ZIP attachment to each node
ladders.why: Image Streaming overlays eligible Artifact Registry layers via a network mount so the container entrypoint starts immediately using only the few megabytes needed at boot.

ladders.title: Cloud Run High-Concurrency Request Autoscaling
ladders.quip: "Each container instance served 80 concurrent HTTP/2 requests—scaled from 0 to 400 instances in seconds during peak traffic!"
ladders.tip: Tune `--concurrency` on Cloud Run Services for stateless I/O-bound APIs so fewer container instances handle more simultaneous requests at lower cost.
ladders.docLabel: Set Maximum Concurrent Requests per Instance
ladders.q: When should you lower `--concurrency` (e.g., to `1` or `4`) vs keep a higher concurrency (e.g., `80`) on a Cloud Run Service?
opts: Always set `--concurrency=1000` for single-threaded CPU-bound video transcoding
Use higher concurrency (`80+`) for thread-safe, async I/O-bound APIs, and lower concurrency (`1`–`4`) for CPU-bound, memory-heavy, or non-thread-safe workloads
Concurrency settings only change the font size in Cloud Logging
ladders.why: High concurrency multiplexes I/O wait time efficiently on async web servers, whereas CPU-heavy or non-thread-safe code needs low concurrency to avoid contention or OOMs.

ladders.title: Cloud Run Jobs with Parallel Array Tasks (`CLOUD_RUN_TASK_INDEX`)
ladders.quip: "Sharded a nightly 2-hour billing reconciliation across 100 parallel Cloud Run Job tasks—completed in 90 seconds with zero idle VMs!"
ladders.tip: Use Cloud Run Jobs with `--tasks=N` and the injected `CLOUD_RUN_TASK_INDEX` environment variable to partition batch datasets across parallel containers.
ladders.docLabel: Create and Execute Cloud Run Jobs
ladders.q: How does each parallel container instance in a multi-task Cloud Run Job know which shard of work to process?
opts: It reads the built-in `CLOUD_RUN_TASK_INDEX` and `CLOUD_RUN_TASK_COUNT` environment variables injected automatically into each task container
It listens on HTTP port 80 for a load balancer cookie
All tasks must process the exact same rows and overwrite each other
ladders.why: Cloud Run Jobs inject `CLOUD_RUN_TASK_INDEX` (`0..N-1`) and `CLOUD_RUN_TASK_COUNT` (`N`) so each task deterministically processes its own slice.

ladders.title: Cloud Run Startup CPU Boost & Warm `--min-instances`
ladders.quip: "Enabled Startup CPU Boost and 2 warm `--min-instances`—Java Spring Boot cold-start p99 dropped by 65%!"
ladders.tip: Enable `--cpu-boost` on Cloud Run to temporarily double/increase vCPU during container initialization and pair with `--min-instances` for latency-sensitive APIs.
ladders.docLabel: Configure Startup CPU Boost in Cloud Run
ladders.q: What does enabling Startup CPU Boost (`--cpu-boost`) do on a Cloud Run Service?
opts: It permanently triples the memory limit of the container for 30 days
It disables TLS encryption on the load balancer
It temporarily allocates extra vCPU during container instance startup and for a short period after the first request arrives, speeding up runtime/JIT initialization
ladders.why: Startup CPU Boost gives JVM, .NET, Node, and Python runtimes extra CPU headroom during class loading and JIT warm-up without paying for over-provisioned CPU all day.

ladders.title: Cloud Run Direct VPC Egress (No Connector VM Bottleneck)
ladders.quip: "Switched from legacy Serverless VPC Access connectors to Direct VPC Egress—cut private AlloyDB & Redis latency while eliminating connector VM costs!"
ladders.tip: Use Direct VPC Egress on Cloud Run to send traffic directly into your VPC subnet with higher throughput, lower latency, and no intermediate connector VMs.
ladders.docLabel: Direct VPC Egress with Cloud Run
ladders.q: What is the primary architectural advantage of Cloud Run Direct VPC Egress over a Serverless VPC Access connector?
opts: Traffic flows directly from the Cloud Run container's network interface into your VPC subnet without traversing proxy connector VMs that incur fixed instance charges and bandwidth caps
It exposes every private VPC database directly to the public internet without authentication
It requires deploying a hardware router in your office
ladders.why: Direct VPC Egress assigns subnet IPs directly to Cloud Run instances, removing the throughput bottleneck and always-on VM cost of legacy VPC connectors.

ladders.title: GKE Gateway API (`Gateway` + `HTTPRoute` Canary Weights)
ladders.quip: "Platform Ops owns the shared regional `Gateway` and TLS certs, while app teams safely shift 5% canary traffic in their own namespace `HTTPRoute`!"
ladders.tip: Adopt the Kubernetes Gateway API on GKE for role-oriented separation (`GatewayClass`, `Gateway`, `HTTPRoute`) and native weighted traffic splitting.
ladders.q: How does the Kubernetes Gateway API improve upon the legacy `Ingress` resource in multi-team GKE clusters?
opts: It removes support for HTTPS certificates
It separates infrastructure ownership (`Gateway` managed by Platform/NetOps) from application routing (`HTTPRoute` managed by devs) with built-in header matching and weighted canary splits
It requires every developer to have Organization Admin permissions
ladders.why: Gateway API introduces role-oriented resources (`GatewayClass`, `Gateway`, `HTTPRoute`) and native traffic splitting, header routing, and cross-namespace attachment.

ladders.title: Cloud Service Mesh Managed Control Plane & Auto mTLS
ladders.quip: "Every east-west RPC is mutually authenticated with Mesh CA X.509 workload certificates and enforced by L7 `AuthorizationPolicy`!"
ladders.tip: Use Google-managed Cloud Service Mesh with Mesh CA to enforce zero-trust mTLS, L7 authorization policies, and golden-signal telemetry without operating your own Istio control plane.
ladders.q: How does Google-managed Cloud Service Mesh issue and rotate workload mTLS identities across GKE Pods?
opts: Developers manually generate self-signed `.pem` files on their laptops and copy them via `kubectl cp`
It shares a single static password across all containers in the project
Mesh CA (or Certificate Authority Service) automatically issues and rotates short-lived SPIFFE X.509 certificates bound to each Pod's Kubernetes ServiceAccount via Workload Identity
ladders.why: Cloud Service Mesh automates short-lived SPIFFE certificate issuance and rotation tied to the workload's cryptographic identity (`spiffe://<project>.svc.id.goog/ns/<ns>/sa/<sa>`).

ladders.title: GKE Multi-Cluster Gateway & `ServiceExport` Active-Active
ladders.quip: "Drained an entire `us-east1` GKE cluster for maintenance and global traffic seamlessly shifted to `us-central1` via Multi-Cluster Services!"
ladders.tip: Register clusters to a Fleet and use Multi-Cluster Gateway (`gke-l7-global-external-managed-mc`) with `ServiceExport`/`ServiceImport` for cross-region failover.
ladders.q: Which Kubernetes custom resource exposes a GKE `Service` across Fleet member clusters so a Multi-Cluster `HTTPRoute` can route to it?
opts: `ServiceExport` (paired with the automatically reconciled `ServiceImport`)
`NodePortBroadcast`
`ConfigMapGlobal`
ladders.why: Creating a `ServiceExport` in member clusters registers backend NEGs with the Fleet so Multi-Cluster Services and Multi-Cluster Gateways can route across clusters.

ladders.title: Cloud Deploy Automated Canary Verification & 1-Click Rollback
ladders.quip: "Promoted `dev → staging → prod` with a 10% → 50% → 100% canary strategy and automated post-deploy verification jobs!"
ladders.tip: Use Google Cloud Deploy delivery pipelines with canary phases, approval gates, and verification jobs targeting both GKE and Cloud Run.
ladders.q: What happens in Google Cloud Deploy when an automated verification job fails during the 20% canary phase of a rollout?
opts: It immediately promotes the broken build to 100% of production traffic anyway
The rollout halts at the failed phase without advancing to 100%, allowing a single-command or automated rollback to the previous known-good release
It deletes the entire GKE cluster
ladders.why: Cloud Deploy gates phase progression on verification results; if verification fails during a canary phase, progression stops and operators can roll back cleanly.

ladders.title: Binary Authorization + SLSA Build & Scan Attestations
ladders.quip: "A rogue `kubectl run` with an unsigned Docker Hub image was blocked instantly at admission by Binary Authorization!"
ladders.tip: Enforce Binary Authorization on GKE and Cloud Run to require cryptographic attestations from Cloud Build and Artifact Analysis vulnerability policies.
ladders.q: How does Binary Authorization verify that a container image hasn't been tampered with after passing CI security checks?
opts: It checks that the image tag string contains the word `safe`
It trusts any image pushed from a laptop with `docker push`
It validates cryptographic signatures (attestations) in Artifact Analysis against the immutable image digest (`@sha256:...`) using Cloud KMS public keys at admission time
ladders.why: Attestations are cryptographically signed over the immutable `@sha256` image digest, preventing tag-swap attacks and unauthorized images.

ladders.title: Artifact Registry Remote & Virtual Repos with Immutable Tags
ladders.quip: "Cached upstream public base images inside a regional Artifact Registry Remote repo—immune to upstream rate limits and scanned for CVEs!"
ladders.tip: Use Artifact Registry Remote repositories to proxy/cache upstream registries (Docker Hub, Maven, PyPI) and combine them with private repos via Virtual repositories.
ladders.q: What are the two major benefits of pulling public base images through an Artifact Registry Remote repository instead of directly from Docker Hub?
opts: Upstream artifacts are cached regionally inside Google Cloud (avoiding external rate limits/egress) and automatically scanned by Artifact Analysis for vulnerabilities
It converts Python code into Rust automatically
It bypasses all IAM permissions in the organization
ladders.why: Remote repositories act as an authenticated, vulnerability-scanned regional pull-through cache for public package and container registries.

ladders.title: Workload Identity Federation for GKE (Direct IAM Principal Binding)
ladders.tip: Grant IAM roles directly to Kubernetes ServiceAccount principals via Workload Identity Federation for GKE rather than exporting service account keys.
ladders.q: With modern Workload Identity Federation for GKE, what is the recommended way to grant a Kubernetes ServiceAccount access to a Cloud Storage bucket?
opts: Create a downloadable service account JSON key and mount it as a Kubernetes Secret

Grant the IAM role directly to the Kubernetes ServiceAccount `principal://iam.googleapis.com/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/PROJECT_ID.svc.id.goog/subject/ns/NAMESPACE/sa/KSA_NAME`
Grant `roles/owner` to the Compute Engine default node service account
ladders.why: Direct IAM bindings to the GKE Workload Identity pool principal eliminate both JSON keys and the need to manage intermediate IAM Service Account impersonation bindings.

ladders.title: Secret Manager CSI Driver & Cloud Run Secret Volume Mounts
ladders.quip: "Mounted pinned Secret Manager versions onto in-memory tmpfs volumes—zero secrets stored in etcd or leaked in environment dumps!"
ladders.tip: Mount secrets from Secret Manager as files (via the Secret Manager CSI Driver on GKE or Secret Volume Mounts on Cloud Run) instead of plaintext environment variables.
ladders.docLabel: Use Secret Manager Add-on with GKE
ladders.q: Why is mounting secrets as files from Secret Manager safer than injecting them as environment variables (`env:`)?
opts: Environment variables are often accidentally logged in startup diagnostics, crash dumps, or child processes, whereas volume-mounted secrets stay off `os.environ` and can support rotation
Environment variables cannot store strings longer than 4 characters
Volume mounts automatically publish secrets to GitHub
ladders.why: Mounting secrets via the Secret Manager CSI driver or Cloud Run volume mounts avoids exposing secrets in process environment dumps and supports refreshing rotated secrets.

ladders.title: Dedicated `startupProbe` + Lightweight `livenessProbe`
ladders.quip: "Separated slow 45-second cache warm-up into a `startupProbe` so `livenessProbe` stays fast without causing a restart death spiral!"
ladders.tip: Use `startupProbe` to accommodate slow initialization (migrations, model loading, JIT warm-up) and keep `livenessProbe` fast and local.
ladders.docLabel: Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes
ladders.q: How do `startupProbe`, `readinessProbe`, and `livenessProbe` work together during a container's lifecycle?
opts: All three probes run in parallel from millisecond zero and kill the node if any fail
`livenessProbe` and `readinessProbe` wait until `startupProbe` succeeds; `readinessProbe` controls load-balancer traffic eligibility, while `livenessProbe` restarts deadlocked containers
`readinessProbe` deletes the container image from Artifact Registry on failure
ladders.why: `startupProbe` gates the start of `livenessProbe` so slow-starting apps aren't killed prematurely; `readinessProbe` removes overloaded pods from endpoints without restarting them.

ladders.title: `topologySpreadConstraints` + `PodDisruptionBudget`
ladders.quip: "Replicas stayed balanced across 3 zones (`maxSkew: 1`) and `PodDisruptionBudget` guaranteed 80% availability during node upgrades!"
ladders.tip: Pair `topologySpreadConstraints` across `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` with a `PodDisruptionBudget` so neither zone outages nor voluntary drains take down your service.
ladders.docLabel: Pod Topology Spread Constraints on GKE
ladders.q: What happens if you deploy 6 replicas in a regional GKE cluster without `topologySpreadConstraints` or pod anti-affinity?
opts: GKE refuses to schedule more than 1 replica per region
Kubernetes automatically replicates pods across AWS and Azure
The scheduler may bin-pack all 6 replicas onto a single node or a single availability zone, creating a single point of failure during a zonal outage
ladders.why: Without explicit `topologySpreadConstraints` across `topology.kubernetes.io/zone`, bin-packing can place all replicas in one zone.

snakes.title: Container `OOMKilled` (Exit 137) from Unbounded JVM/Node Heap
snakes.quip: "Set container memory limit to `1Gi` but forgot `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0`—the JVM allocated off-heap metaspace past 1 GiB and the kernel `OOMKilled` every pod under load!"
snakes.tip: Size language runtime heaps (`-XX:MaxRAMPercentage`, `--max-old-space-size`, `GOMEMLIMIT`) to 70%–80% of the container `resources.limits.memory` to leave headroom for off-heap/native memory.
snakes.prevent: Set container-aware runtime heap limits (`-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0` or `GOMEMLIMIT`) and set `resources.requests.memory == resources.limits.memory` (Guaranteed QoS for memory).
snakes.detect: Cloud Monitoring alert on `kubernetes.io/container/memory/used_bytes` approaching limit and `reason: OOMKilled` (Exit Code 137) events.
snakes.recover: Increase memory request/limit via VPA recommendations and cap runtime heap below the container cgroup limit.
snakes.q: Why do Java, Node.js, or Go containers frequently get `OOMKilled` (exit code 137) even when their configured max heap size equals 100% of the container memory limit?
opts: Runtimes also consume native off-heap memory (thread stacks, metaspace, direct byte buffers, GC overhead) inside the same cgroup limit; heap should be capped at ~70–80% of container memory
Kubernetes adds 5 GB of random log files into RAM every minute
Exit code 137 means DNS resolution succeeded
snakes.why: The Linux cgroup memory limit covers heap + thread stacks + native buffers + metaspace; leaving 20–30% headroom prevents kernel OOM kills.

snakes.title: Aggressive CFS CPU Limit (`limits.cpu: 200m`) Spiked p99 Latency
snakes.quip: "Multi-threaded Go pods finished their 20ms CPU quota in the first 3ms of each 100ms Linux CFS period and sat throttled for the remaining 97ms!"
snakes.tip: Set accurate `resources.requests.cpu` so pods get guaranteed CPU shares, and avoid tight `resources.limits.cpu` on latency-sensitive multi-threaded services.
snakes.prevent: Size `resources.requests.cpu` accurately for burst concurrency and omit or relax restrictive `limits.cpu` on GKE Standard latency-critical services.
snakes.detect: Monitor `container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total / container_cpu_cfs_periods_total` in Cloud Monitoring Managed Service for Prometheus.
snakes.recover: Raise `requests.cpu` and remove or widen restrictive `limits.cpu` so multi-threaded request bursts are not paused by CFS quota enforcement.
snakes.docLabel: Adjust Pod CPU and Memory Sizing
snakes.q: Why can setting a low `resources.limits.cpu` (e.g., `200m`) on an 8-thread web server cause severe p99 latency spikes even when node CPU is 70% idle?
opts: Kubernetes shuts down the network card whenever `limits.cpu` is set
All 8 threads burn through the 20ms per-100ms Linux CFS quota in a few milliseconds and the kernel throttles the container until the next 100ms period
Low CPU limits disable HTTPS encryption
snakes.why: Linux CFS enforces `limits.cpu` across all threads per 100ms window; parallel threads exhaust a small quota rapidly and stall for the remainder of the window.

snakes.title: VPC-Native GKE Pod Secondary CIDR Range Exhausted (`/24`)
snakes.quip: "Configured a tiny `/24` secondary IP range for Pods—node autoscaling failed with `IP_SPACE_EXHAUSTED` because every node reserves a `/24` alias range!"
snakes.tip: Size GKE Pod secondary CIDR ranges generously (or use discontinuous multi-pod CIDR ranges and lower `--max-pods-per-node`) before scaling.
snakes.prevent: Provision a `/17`–`/20` secondary Pod CIDR range (or reduce max Pods per node so each node reserves a `/25` or `/26` instead of a full `/24`).
snakes.detect: Cloud Monitoring alert on `networking.googleapis.com/subnet/ip_utilization` and GKE Cluster Autoscaler `scale.up.error.ip.space.exhausted` events.
snakes.recover: Add an additional Pod IP CIDR range to the cluster (`--additional-pod-ipv4-ranges`) without recreating the cluster.
snakes.q: How can you expand Pod IP capacity on a live VPC-native GKE cluster when the initial Pod secondary CIDR range fills up?
opts: Delete the entire VPC and rebuild production from scratch
Disable IP addresses and route Pods using MAC addresses across the internet
Add a new secondary IPv4 range to the subnet and attach it to the cluster or node pool using multi-Pod CIDR (`--additional-pod-ipv4-ranges`)
snakes.why: GKE supports adding discontinuous secondary Pod IPv4 ranges dynamically (`--additional-pod-ipv4-ranges`) and tuning `maxPodsPerNode` to reduce per-node CIDR block size.

snakes.title: Single-Zone GKE Cluster Outage During Control Plane Upgrade
snakes.quip: "Provisioned a zonal GKE Standard cluster in `us-central1-a`—control plane API paused during upgrades and a single zone impairment took down all nodes!"
snakes.tip: Always use Regional GKE clusters (or GKE Autopilot, which is regional by default) for production workloads so both the control plane and worker nodes span 3 zones.
snakes.prevent: Provision Regional GKE Standard or GKE Autopilot clusters with multi-zone node locations.
snakes.detect: GKE Security Posture and Architecture Framework checks flagging single-zone production clusters.
snakes.recover: Stand up a Regional GKE cluster, register both to a GKE Fleet, shift traffic via Multi-Cluster Gateway or Cloud DNS, and retire the zonal cluster.
snakes.docLabel: GKE Cluster Types: Regional vs Zonal
snakes.q: What happens to the Kubernetes API control plane during a master upgrade on a Zonal GKE cluster vs a Regional GKE cluster?
opts: A Zonal cluster has a single control plane instance that is temporarily unavailable during upgrades, whereas a Regional cluster replicates the control plane across 3 zones for zero-downtime API availability
Regional clusters shut down all Pods during upgrades
Zonal clusters replicate their control plane across 12 continents
snakes.why: Regional GKE clusters run three control plane replicas across three zones in the region, keeping `kube-apiserver` andautoscalers online during upgrades and single-zone failures.

snakes.title: Background Async Task Frozen After HTTP `200 OK` Response
snakes.quip: "Returned `200 OK` immediately and spawned a background thread to upload the invoice—under default request-based billing, CPU was throttled to near-zero the millisecond the HTTP response finished!"
snakes.tip: Under Cloud Run request-based CPU billing (`--cpu-throttling`), never run background work after returning the HTTP response; either await completion, offload to Pub/Sub / Cloud Tasks, or enable `--no-cpu-throttling`.
snakes.prevent: Offload async work to Cloud Tasks / Pub/Sub before returning the HTTP response, or enable instance-based billing (`--no-cpu-throttling`) if short background work is required.
snakes.detect: Cloud Trace spans and logs showing background tasks freezing after HTTP response completion and finishing only when the next inbound request wakes the container.
snakes.recover: Enable `--no-cpu-throttling` (CPU always allocated) immediately to unfreeze in-flight background threads, then refactor to Cloud Tasks or Pub/Sub.
snakes.q: Why did a background goroutine/thread started inside a Cloud Run HTTP handler stall right after the handler sent `200 OK`?
opts: Go and Python threads are blocked by Cloud Armor
With default request-based CPU allocation (`--cpu-throttling`), Cloud Run throttles container CPU to near-zero whenever no HTTP request is actively being processed
Cloud Run deletes the container image after every HTTP status 200
snakes.why: By default, Cloud Run allocates CPU only while at least one request is open on the instance; post-response background work requires `--no-cpu-throttling` or an async queue like Cloud Tasks.

snakes.title: Cloud Run Scaled to 800 Instances and Exhausted `max_connections`
snakes.quip: "Left `--max-instances` uncapped with a 10-connection SQL pool per container—a traffic surge opened 8,000 PostgreSQL connections and crashed the database!"
snakes.tip: Cap `--max-instances` on Cloud Run, keep per-instance DB pool sizes small (`1`–`5`), and route through managed connection pooling / PgBouncer.
snakes.prevent: Set explicit `--max-instances`, size per-container DB pools so `max_instances × pool_size < DB max_connections`, and use PgBouncer / AlloyDB connection pooling.
snakes.detect: Cloud Monitoring alert on `database/postgresql/num_backends` and Cloud Run `500` errors with `FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved`.
snakes.recover: Lower `--max-instances`, reduce the per-container SQL pool size to 2–5, and enable managed connection pooling.
snakes.docLabel: Set Maximum Instances in Cloud Run
snakes.q: How do you prevent a sudden Cloud Run scale-out from exhausting a downstream Cloud SQL or AlloyDB database's connection limit?
opts: Set the per-container connection pool size to 500
Disable autoscaling by setting `--max-instances=1` for all production traffic
Bound `--max-instances`, keep per-instance connection pools small, increase HTTP `--concurrency` per instance, and use a connection pooler like PgBouncer
snakes.why: Higher HTTP concurrency per instance reduces total container count, while bounded `--max-instances` and PgBouncer transaction pooling protect database connection limits.

snakes.title: Writing 600 MB CSV Export to `/tmp` Crashed 512 MiB Cloud Run Instance
snakes.quip: "Wrote a temporary 600 MB report to `/tmp/report.csv` before uploading to Cloud Storage—forgot that Cloud Run's `/tmp` is an in-memory `tmpfs` backed by container RAM!"
snakes.tip: Remember that writable filesystem paths (like `/tmp`) in Cloud Run are stored in container memory (`tmpfs`); stream large payloads directly to Cloud Storage or delete `/tmp` files immediately.
snakes.prevent: Use streaming multipart uploads directly to Cloud Storage (or Signed URLs so clients upload directly to GCS) and unlink temporary files immediately.
snakes.detect: Cloud Run `run.googleapis.com/container/memory/utilizations` climbing monotonically across requests followed by memory limit termination.
snakes.recover: Stream data directly to/from Cloud Storage without buffering full files in `/tmp`, and increase `--memory` if local scratch space is unavoidable.
snakes.q: Where are files written to `/tmp` stored inside a Cloud Run container instance?
opts: In an in-memory `tmpfs` filesystem that counts directly against the container instance's configured memory limit
On an unlimited free 100 TB local NVMe disk
Automatically inside BigQuery tables
snakes.why: Cloud Run's writable filesystem is an in-memory `tmpfs`; uncleaned or oversized files in `/tmp` consume container RAM and trigger OOM crashes.

snakes.title: Synchronous Chain of 5 Cloud Run Services Compounded Cold Starts & Cost
snakes.quip: "Service A called Service B synchronously, which waited on C, D, and E—all 5 billed for simultaneous wall-clock wait time and compounded cold-start tail latency to 12 seconds!"
snakes.tip: Avoid deep synchronous HTTP chains across serverless services; decouple stages asynchronously with Pub/Sub, Cloud Tasks, or Workflows.
snakes.prevent: Use Cloud Workflows for orchestration or Pub/Sub / Cloud Tasks for asynchronous event-driven handoffs instead of nested blocking HTTP calls.
snakes.detect: Cloud Trace waterfalls showing outer Cloud Run spans sitting idle waiting on nested downstream HTTP calls.
snakes.recover: Break synchronous HTTP chains into asynchronous Pub/Sub / Cloud Tasks steps or consolidate tightly coupled internal hops.
snakes.q: What are the two major downsides of chaining 5 Cloud Run services synchronously (`A → B → C → D → E`) in a blocking HTTP call tree?
opts: Cloud Run blocks HTTP requests between services in the same project
Tail latencies and cold starts add up across all 5 hops, and upstream services remain open billing for request duration while idly waiting on downstream hops
Each hop reduces the payload size by 50%
snakes.why: Synchronous chains compound tail latency/failure probabilities and double-bill for idle upstream wait time; async queues or Workflows eliminate blocking wait chains.

snakes.title: Rolling Deployment `502 Bad Gateway` Spikes During Pod Termination
snakes.quip: "Every rolling update dropped 1% of requests with `502 Bad Gateway` because Pods closed their HTTP listener immediately on `SIGTERM` before the Google Cloud Load Balancer removed the NEG endpoint!"
snakes.tip: Add a `preStop` sleep hook (e.g., `sleep 10`–`15`) and keep the HTTP server accepting in-flight connections briefly while the GCLB NEG health check deregisters the terminating Pod.
snakes.prevent: Configure a `lifecycle.preStop` hook (`sleep 15`), mark readiness failing on `SIGTERM`, and set `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60`.
snakes.detect: Cloud Load Balancing logs showing `statusDetails: backend_connection_closed_before_data_sent_to_client` (`502`) correlated with GKE rolling updates.
snakes.recover: Add `lifecycle.preStop: exec: command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 15"]` and graceful HTTP server drain on `SIGTERM`.
snakes.q: Why do GKE Services backed by Container-Native Load Balancing (NEGs) sometimes return `502 Bad Gateway` during Pod scale-in or rolling updates if no `preStop` hook is configured?
opts: GKE deletes the entire VPC firewall during every rolling update
Container-Native Load Balancing only supports UDP traffic

Endpoint removal propagation to the external Envoy/GFE load balancer runs asynchronously in parallel with `SIGTERM`; if the Pod closes its socket immediately, in-flight LB requests hit a closed socket
snakes.why: When a Pod terminates, NEG endpoint deregistration and `SIGTERM` happen concurrently; a brief `preStop` delay lets the load balancer drain traffic before the app closes its listening socket.

snakes.title: Cluster-Wide `STRICT` mTLS Applied Without `PERMISSIVE` Migration Window
snakes.quip: "Applied a root-namespace `PeerAuthentication` with `mtls.mode: STRICT` on Friday afternoon—instantly broke every non-mesh client and external health check!"
snakes.tip: Migrate to Cloud Service Mesh mTLS gradually: start in `PERMISSIVE` mode (accepting both plaintext and mTLS), verify 100% mTLS coverage in metrics, then lock down to `STRICT` per namespace.
snakes.prevent: Roll out `PeerAuthentication` in `PERMISSIVE` mode first, audit plaintext connections via mesh telemetry, and transition to `STRICT` namespace-by-namespace.
snakes.detect: Cloud Service Mesh metrics (`istio_requests_total` with `connection_security_policy="none"`) identifying remaining plaintext callers before enforcing `STRICT`.
snakes.recover: Revert `PeerAuthentication` to `PERMISSIVE` to restore traffic, onboard remaining callers to the mesh, then re-enable `STRICT`.
snakes.docLabel: Cloud Service Mesh Mutual TLS Migration
snakes.q: What is the recommended migration path to enforce `STRICT` mutual TLS in Cloud Service Mesh without causing an outage?
opts: Start in `PERMISSIVE` mode (which accepts both plaintext and mTLS), use mesh telemetry to confirm all callers use mTLS, and then switch to `STRICT` per namespace/workload
Switch the entire production fleet to `STRICT` at peak traffic without sidecars
Disable TLS completely and use telnet
snakes.why: `PERMISSIVE` mode allows sidecar-injected workloads to negotiate mTLS while still accepting plaintext from unmigrated callers until 100% mesh coverage is verified.

snakes.title: Private GKE Pods Pulled Container Images via Cloud NAT Public IPs
snakes.quip: "Left Private Google Access disabled on the GKE subnet—every private node pulled multi-gigabyte Artifact Registry images and GCS blobs through Cloud NAT at $0.045/GB!"
snakes.tip: Always enable Private Google Access (or Private Service Connect for Google APIs) on subnets hosting GKE nodes and Cloud Run Direct VPC Egress.
snakes.prevent: Enable `Private Google Access` on all VPC subnets via Terraform and enforce via Org Policy / network modules.
snakes.detect: Cloud Billing spike in `Cloud NAT Data Processed` paired with VPC Flow Logs showing traffic to Google API IP ranges traversing the NAT gateway.
snakes.recover: Enable Private Google Access (`gcloud compute networks subnets update --enable-private-ip-google-access`) so Google API traffic stays on Google's private network free of NAT processing fees.
snakes.q: Why were private GKE nodes incurring thousands of dollars in Cloud NAT data-processing charges when pulling images from Artifact Registry in the same region?
opts: Artifact Registry only works over dial-up modems
Private Google Access was disabled on the GKE subnet, forcing traffic destined for `*.pkg.dev` and `*.googleapis.com` out through the paid Cloud NAT gateway
GKE Autopilot requires 10 Cloud NAT gateways per Pod
snakes.why: Enabling Private Google Access routes traffic to Artifact Registry and Cloud Storage over Google's internal network without using or paying for Cloud NAT.

snakes.title: Mutable `:latest` Tag Caused Split-Brain Pods During Autoscaling
snakes.quip: "Deployed `image: app:latest`—when HPA scaled out from 5 to 20 Pods two hours later, the 15 new Pods pulled an unreviewed dev push overwritten onto `:latest`!"
snakes.tip: Pin every production GKE and Cloud Run deployment to an immutable `@sha256:...` image digest and enable tag immutability on Artifact Registry.
snakes.prevent: Enable immutable tags on Artifact Registry, deploy by immutable digest (`image@sha256:...`), and block mutable tags via Policy Controller / Binary Authorization.
snakes.detect: GKE Security Posture and Policy Controller `K8sImageDigests` constraint violations flagging images without `@sha256:` digests.
snakes.recover: Roll back the Deployment to the pinned `@sha256:` digest of the known-good release and enable tag immutability in Artifact Registry.
snakes.q: What is the risk of referencing a mutable tag like `:latest` or `:prod` in a Kubernetes Deployment manifest?
opts: Kubernetes cannot parse colons in image strings
Every node caches `:latest` forever even when `imagePullPolicy: Always` is set
When HPA scales out or a node reschedules a Pod later, new Pods may pull a different image binary than existing Pods, causing version drift and breaking rollbacks
snakes.why: Deploying by immutable digest (`@sha256:...`) guarantees every replica runs the exact same verified container binary across scale-outs and rollbacks.

snakes.title: `privileged: true` Pod with `hostPath: /` Escaped to Worker Node
snakes.quip: "A debugging manifest with `securityContext.privileged: true` and `hostPath: /` made it to prod—giving a compromised container full root access to the GKE node and kubelet credentials!"
snakes.tip: Enforce the Kubernetes `Restricted` Pod Security Standard (`pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted`) or use GKE Autopilot, which blocks `privileged: true` and `hostPath` by default.
snakes.prevent: Use GKE Autopilot or enforce Pod Security Admission (`restricted` profile) and Policy Controller constraints blocking `privileged`, `hostPath`, and `hostNetwork`.
snakes.detect: Security Command Center / GKE Security Posture findings (`PRIVILEGED_CONTAINER`, `HOST_PATH_VOLUME_MOUNT`) and Cloud Audit Logs on `pods/create`.
snakes.recover: Evict the privileged Pod, cordone/replace the affected node pool VMs, rotate credentials, and enforce the `restricted` Pod Security Standard.
snakes.docLabel: Enforce Pod Security Standards in GKE
snakes.q: Which built-in Kubernetes admission control mechanism blocks `privileged: true`, `hostPath` mounts, and root user execution at the namespace level?
opts: Pod Security Standards (`pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted`) via the built-in Pod Security Admission controller
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
kube-proxy iptables mode
snakes.why: Pod Security Admission enforces the `baseline` or `restricted` Pod Security Standard natively on namespaces without requiring third-party webhook infrastructure.

snakes.title: GKE Nodes Created with Default Compute Service Account (`roles/editor`)
snakes.quip: "Created a GKE Standard node pool without a custom IAM service account or Workload Identity—every Pod on the node inherited `PROJECT_NUMBER-compute@developer` with project-wide `Editor` access!"
snakes.tip: Always enable Workload Identity Federation for GKE and assign a minimally privileged custom IAM service account (`roles/container.defaultNodeServiceAccount`) to node pools.
snakes.prevent: Enforce `constraints/iam.automaticIamGrantsForDefaultServiceAccounts`, use a dedicated node SA with `roles/container.defaultNodeServiceAccount`, and enable Workload Identity.
snakes.detect: GKE Security Posture and Security Command Center `NODE_POOL_USES_DEFAULT_SERVICE_ACCOUNT` findings.
snakes.recover: Enable Workload Identity on the cluster, migrate node pools to a least-privilege custom node service account, and bind Pods to scoped IAM principals.
snakes.q: Which minimally privileged predefined IAM role should be granted to a custom GKE node pool service account instead of `roles/editor`?
opts: `roles/owner`
`roles/container.defaultNodeServiceAccount` (plus Artifact Registry Reader if pulling private images)
`roles/iam.securityAdmin`
snakes.why: `roles/container.defaultNodeServiceAccount` contains only the minimum logging, monitoring, and node telemetry permissions required by the GKE kubelet.

snakes.title: Plaintext Database & Stripe Keys Committed in `Deployment.yaml`
snakes.quip: "Hardcoded `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` inside `Deployment.yaml` and printed `process.env` on startup—leaked production credentials into Git history and Cloud Logging!"
snakes.tip: Never store credentials in Git manifests or log `process.env`; store secrets in Secret Manager and mount them via CSI driver or Cloud Run Secret volumes.
snakes.prevent: Store all credentials in Secret Manager, mount as files via CSI/Cloud Run secret integration, and run pre-commit secret scanning in CI.
snakes.detect: Secret scanning alerts in CI/Git and Cloud Logging DLP inspection / log exclusion filters.
snakes.recover: Rotate the compromised API keys immediately in Secret Manager, purge the plaintext logs/history, and switch the workload to Secret Manager volume mounts.
snakes.q: What is the best practice for providing a sensitive third-party API key to a Cloud Run Service or GKE Pod?
opts: Commit the API key into a public `ConfigMap` in Git
Pass it in the URL query string of every user request
Store it in Google Cloud Secret Manager, pin the workload to a specific secret version, and mount it as a volume (or secret reference) via least-privilege IAM
snakes.why: Secret Manager provides encryption at rest, audit logging, IAM access control, and version pinning so secrets never live in Git or plaintext manifests.

snakes.title: `livenessProbe` Querying Shared Database Triggered Cascading Restart Loop
snakes.quip: "Pointed `livenessProbe` at `/healthz` which ran `SELECT 1` on PostgreSQL—a 2-second DB blip caused kubelet to restart all 50 Pods simultaneously, DDOSing the DB on boot!"
snakes.tip: Never check external downstream dependencies inside a `livenessProbe`; `livenessProbe` should only verify the local process is not deadlocked.
snakes.prevent: Keep `livenessProbe` strictly local (checking only that the local HTTP/gRPC event loop responds) and reserve dependency checks for `readinessProbe` or circuit breakers.
snakes.detect: High Pod restart counts (`kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total`) occurring simultaneously across all replicas during brief downstream latency spikes.
snakes.recover: Change `livenessProbe` to hit a lightweight local `/livez` endpoint that does not call external databases or downstream APIs.
snakes.docLabel: Configure Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes
snakes.q: Why should a `livenessProbe` NEVER fail when a downstream database or external API is temporarily slow?
opts: Failing `livenessProbe` restarts the container—restarting all healthy application Pods won't fix an external database blip and instead triggers a thundering-herd cold-start outage
`livenessProbe` is billed at $10 per failure
`livenessProbe` can only check UDP ports
snakes.why: A `livenessProbe` failure kills and restarts the Pod; only local unrecoverable deadlocks warrant a restart, while external dependency issues should be handled via `readinessProbe` or circuit breakers.

snakes.title: `PodDisruptionBudget` with `maxUnavailable: 0` Blocked Node Pool Security Patching
snakes.quip: "Set `minAvailable: 100%` (`maxUnavailable: 0`) on a 3-replica Deployment—GKE node upgrades and autoscaler scale-down could never evict a single Pod and timed out!"
snakes.tip: Always leave at least 1 Pod of eviction budget in every `PodDisruptionBudget` (e.g., `maxUnavailable: 1` or `minAvailable: 80%` with >= 2 replicas).
snakes.prevent: Set `maxUnavailable: 1` (or `25%`) on multi-replica Deployments and validate PDBs in CI with Policy Controller.
snakes.recover: Update the `PodDisruptionBudget` to `maxUnavailable: 1` (or `minAvailable: N-1`) so voluntary node drains can proceed safely one Pod at a time.
snakes.docLabel: Ensure Disruption Budget Availability on GKE
snakes.q: What happens if you configure a `PodDisruptionBudget` with `maxUnavailable: 0` (or `minAvailable: 1` on a `replicas: 1` Deployment)?
opts: The Pod becomes 100% immune to hardware failures
Voluntary evictions via the Eviction API (node upgrades, node pool drains, Cluster Autoscaler scale-in) are blocked until the drain timeout expires and forces termination
GKE automatically scales the Deployment to 100 replicas
snakes.why: A zero-disruption budget forbids all voluntary evictions, stalling node maintenance and Cluster Autoscaler scale-down until forced drain timeouts.

snakes.title: Shell Form `ENTRYPOINT "sh -c ./app"` Swallowed `SIGTERM` Signal
snakes.quip: "Used shell form `ENTRYPOINT ./server` so `/bin/sh` ran as PID 1—it ignored `SIGTERM` on scale-in, hung for the full 30s grace period, and got violently `SIGKILL`ed mid-transaction!"
snakes.tip: Always use JSON `exec` array syntax (`ENTRYPOINT ["./server"]`) or `exec` in wrapper scripts so your application runs as PID 1 and receives `SIGTERM` directly.
snakes.prevent: Use `ENTRYPOINT ["/app/server"]` (exec form) or `tini`/`dumb-init` as PID 1, and register a `SIGTERM` handler that drains in-flight requests cleanly.
snakes.detect: Pod termination duration consistently equaling the exact `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` (e.g., 30.0s) followed by `Exit Code 137` (`SIGKILL`).
snakes.recover: Switch the Dockerfile `ENTRYPOINT`/`CMD` to `exec` array form (`["/app/server"]`) so the process runs as PID 1 and handles `SIGTERM` immediately.
snakes.q: Why does a container using `CMD /bin/sh -c "node server.js"` fail to shut down gracefully when GKE or Cloud Run sends `SIGTERM`?
opts: Node.js does not support signals on Linux
`SIGTERM` is only sent to Windows containers
`/bin/sh` runs as PID 1 and does not forward `SIGTERM` to child processes by default, so `node` never receives the signal until `SIGKILL` forcibly terminates the container
snakes.why: Using `ENTRYPOINT ["node", "server.js"]` (or `exec node server.js` in a script) replaces the shell so your app is PID 1 and receives `SIGTERM` directly.

shields.title: Pod Disruption Budgets (`maxUnavailable: 1`)
shields.quip: "Node pool upgrade drained worker VMs one by one while guaranteeing at least 85% of replicas stayed `Ready`!"
shields.tip: Define a `PodDisruptionBudget` for every stateless and stateful service so voluntary node drains never exceed safe capacity limits.

shields.title: Pod Security Standards (`Restricted` Profile)
shields.quip: "Namespace labels enforced non-root execution, dropped `ALL` Linux capabilities, and blocked privilege escalation at admission!"
shields.tip: Label production namespaces with `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted` to enforce least-privilege container security contexts.
shields.docLabel: Enforce Pod Security Standards in GKE

shields.title: Binary Authorization Continuous Validation
shields.quip: "Every container admitted to GKE and Cloud Run is cryptographically attested by Cloud Build with zero critical CVEs!"
shields.tip: Combine Binary Authorization admission enforcement with Continuous Validation (CV) to audit running pods against your attestation policy.

shields.title: Artifact Analysis On-Push OS & Language CVE Scanning
shields.quip: "Caught a critical OpenSSL & Maven dependency CVE the second the image pushed to Artifact Registry—before it ever reached staging!"
shields.tip: Enable Artifact Analysis automatic scanning on Artifact Registry to detect OS and language package vulnerabilities (Go, Java, Node, Python) on push.

shields.title: GKE Release Channels + Maintenance Exclusions
shields.quip: "Enrolled production in the Regular Release Channel with a Black Friday maintenance exclusion window—zero surprise upgrades during peak week!"
shields.tip: Enroll GKE clusters in Release Channels (`Rapid` for dev, `Regular`/`Stable` for prod) and configure Maintenance Windows and Exclusions around peak events.

shields.title: GKE Dataplane V2 (Cilium eBPF) NetworkPolicies
shields.quip: "Default-deny east-west `NetworkPolicy` isolated the `payments` namespace at kernel eBPF speed with built-in packet-drop observability!"
shields.tip: Use GKE Dataplane V2 (powered by Cilium eBPF) and enforce default-deny ingress/egress `NetworkPolicy` manifests between namespaces.

shields.title: Cloud Run Warm Minimum Instances (`--min-instances`)
shields.quip: "Pre-warmed 3 Cloud Run instances with initialized DB pools—zero cold-start penalty for the first morning traffic wave!"
shields.tip: Configure `--min-instances` (or scheduled warm-up scaling) on latency-critical Cloud Run Services to eliminate cold starts.
shields.docLabel: Configure Minimum Instances in Cloud Run

shields.title: Cloud Run Internal Ingress + Cloud Load Balancing + IAP
shields.quip: "Locked down `--ingress=internal-and-cloud-load-balancing` behind Cloud Armor and Identity-Aware Proxy—direct `.run.app` bypass blocked!"
shields.tip: Restrict Cloud Run ingress to `internal-and-cloud-load-balancing` (or disable the default `.run.app` URL) when fronting services with a Global External Application Load Balancer.
shields.docLabel: Restrict Network Ingress for Cloud Run

shields.title: Backup for GKE (Cluster State + Volume Snapshots)
shields.quip: "Scheduled daily encrypted backups of both Kubernetes API manifests and PersistentVolume disks with cross-region retention locks!"
shields.tip: Enable Backup for GKE with automated schedules and locked retention policies to recover namespaces, CRDs, and stateful volumes rapidly.

shields.title: GKE Policy Controller (Shift-Left CI + Admission Guardrails)
shields.quip: "Validated every YAML against OPA Policy Controller constraints in Cloud Build CI and at `kube-apiserver` admission!"
shields.tip: Use Policy Controller to enforce organization-wide constraints (required labels, resource requests, approved registries, no `:latest` tags) in both CI and cluster admission.

shields.title: Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) Rightsizing Guardrail
shields.quip: "VPA historical percentile recommendations eliminated both OOMKills on under-sized pods and 60% slack on over-requested pods!"
shields.tip: Run Vertical Pod Autoscaler in `Off` (recommendation) or `Auto` mode to right-size Pod CPU and memory requests based on real usage.

shields.title: GKE Security Posture Dashboard & Workload Audit
shields.quip: "Continuously scanned running workloads against CIS GKE Benchmarks and Pod Security Standards with actionable remediation guidance!"
shields.tip: Enable the GKE Security Posture dashboard to detect workload configuration risks, RBAC over-permissions, and live container vulnerabilities.

shields.title: `preStop` Drain Hook + Graceful `SIGTERM` Shutdown
shields.quip: "Zero dropped connections during rolling deployments—`preStop` waited for NEG deregistration while the server drained active requests!"
shields.tip: Pair a `preStop` delay with a `SIGTERM` handler that stops accepting new connections and finishes in-flight requests within `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`.

shields.title: Cloud Run CMEK + VPC Service Controls Perimeter
shields.quip: "Encrypted container images and runtime state with Customer-Managed Encryption Keys inside a VPC Service Controls perimeter!"
shields.tip: Protect regulated Cloud Run workloads with Cloud KMS Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK) and VPC Service Controls perimeters.
shields.docLabel: Use Customer-Managed Encryption Keys in Cloud Run

shields.title: NodeLocal DNSCache on GKE
shields.quip: "Cached DNS lookups locally on each GKE node via a DaemonSet—eliminated `kube-dns` conntrack races and cut DNS tail latency to sub-millisecond!"
shields.tip: Enable NodeLocal DNSCache on high-QPS GKE clusters to avoid `kube-dns` bottlenecks and UDP conntrack table exhaustion.
shields.docLabel: Set Up NodeLocal DNSCache on GKE

shields.title: GKE Gateway `GCPBackendPolicy` with Cloud Armor WAF
shields.quip: "Attached an Adaptive Protection Cloud Armor security policy declaratively to our GKE Gateway backends via `GCPBackendPolicy`!"
shields.tip: Attach Cloud Armor security policies, IAP, and custom timeouts to GKE Gateway backends declaratively using `GCPBackendPolicy`.
